clinicalPearls: A rare acquired immunodeficiency of adults defined by the combination of a thymoma and hypogammaglobulinaemia
Typically presents in middle age with recurrent sinopulmonary infections from encapsulated bacteria alongside the antibody deficiency
Opportunistic infections are characteristic, including cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis, mucocutaneous candidiasis, and other pathogens usually seen with T-cell impairment
The immune defect is combined, with low or absent B cells and hypogammaglobulinaemia together with variable T-cell abnormalities such as an inverted CD4 to CD8 ratio
Autoimmune and haematological complications are frequent, including pure red cell aplasia, myasthenia gravis, and cytopenias
Chronic diarrhoea from infective or immune causes and refractory mucocutaneous disease add to the morbidity
Management combines resection of the thymoma, long-term immunoglobulin replacement, and antimicrobial prophylaxis, noting that removing the thymoma does not reverse the immune defect
reference.pathophysiology: Good syndrome links a tumour of the thymic epithelium to a profound acquired immunodeficiency, although the exact mechanism remains incompletely understood. The abnormal thymic microenvironment is thought to disturb lymphocyte development and tolerance, and bone-marrow precursor abnormalities appear to curtail B-cell production, so that mature B cells become scarce and immunoglobulin levels fall. T-cell numbers and function are also perturbed, producing a combined pattern of susceptibility to both encapsulated bacteria (from the antibody failure) and opportunistic organisms (from the cellular defect). The same immune dysregulation, coupled with the thymoma's known association with autoimmunity, underlies the frequent autoimmune cytopenias and neuromuscular disease. Importantly, the immunodeficiency generally persists after the thymoma is removed.
additionalDifferentials: Late-onset combined immunodeficiency of genetic cause
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or other lymphoproliferative disorders with hypogammaglobulinaemia
Secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia from protein loss or drugs
Thymoma with paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes without immunodeficiency
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional chest imaging to identify and characterise the thymoma
Quantitative immunoglobulins with specific antibody responses
B-cell enumeration and lymphocyte subset analysis with CD4 to CD8 ratio
Screening for opportunistic infection including cytomegalovirus and Pneumocystis
Assessment for autoimmune cytopenias and myasthenia gravis (including acetylcholine receptor antibodies)
Bone marrow examination when red cell aplasia or cytopenias are present
Exclusion of HIV and other secondary causes of hypogammaglobulinaemia
redFlags: A newly identified anterior mediastinal mass with recurrent infection
Opportunistic infection such as Pneumocystis or disseminated cytomegalovirus in an adult with low immunoglobulins
Refractory anaemia from pure red cell aplasia
New myasthenic symptoms with a thymoma
Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss and immunodeficiency
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is guarded, with higher infection-related mortality than uncomplicated adult antibody deficiency; immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis reduce infections, but autoimmune complications and opportunistic infection persist because thymoma resection does not correct the immune defect.
pitfalls: Assuming that removing the thymoma will restore immune function
Labelling the antibody deficiency as common variable immunodeficiency without imaging the thymus
Overlooking opportunistic infections by focusing only on the antibody defect
Missing associated autoimmune cytopenias or myasthenia gravis
Delaying immunoglobulin replacement while investigating the tumour
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
